messages.content: In Japanese kintsugi, broken pottery is repaired so the cracks remain visible, often highlighted with gold. What do you make of that idea?

It is an interesting inversion of the usual instinct to hide damage. The repair does not pretend the break never happened; it makes the object's history part of what is visible. I can see why that idea would resonate beyond pottery, even if I would want to learn more before treating my first impression as an understanding of the tradition.

messages.content: Why do people keep old songs alive for generations even when the original events behind them are forgotten?

One possibility is that the song keeps carrying emotion, identity, or social memory even after the exact historical reference fades. I would be cautious about pretending there is one universal reason, though; different traditions probably preserve songs for different combinations of ritual, belonging, pleasure, and remembrance.
So the song can matter even when nobody remembers every original detail?

Yes. Meaning can survive in practice and feeling even when the full origin is no longer available. That does not tell us exactly why any particular community keeps a song, but it helps explain how cultural continuity can outlast precise historical memory.
